features.label: Great Zimbabwe

coordinate.meaning: UNESCO property reference point; not surveyed coordinates of the conical tower
coordinate.uncertainty: Source gives no positional accuracy; decimal conversion adds no accuracy.

features.snapshot_status: Editorial snapshot within the documented building period, after the enclosure's stated century; not an exact construction date.
features.form: An oval Great Enclosure of coursed, cut granite, with a narrow passage toward a conical tower.
features.architecture_gate: An original enclosure-and-tower schematic may represent this later phase. Do not animate the complete enclosure at 1100. The tower itself has no separately verified construction date here; do not give it its own exact-year event.
features.narration: In southern Africa, Great Zimbabwe grew into a major trading city. Its fourteenth-century Great Enclosure still expresses the skill of its stone builders.
excluded_claims: Queen of Sheba legend as history
A single certain cause of abandonment
Modern national boundary as medieval extent

features.label: Kanem, east of Lake Chad
features.site_coordinate_gate: No exact Tié coordinate verified in the opened sources. Do not substitute a similarly named modern locality or interpolate a site point from a small map. Use an explicitly labelled regional view east of Lake Chad; do not render that camera anchor as Njimi.
features.date_interpretation: Modelled two-sigma intervals, not exact years or the founding date of Kanem.
features.snapshot_status: Conservative regional snapshot; the project reports flourishing eleventh–fourteenth-century evidence and the earlier building remained in use into the fourteenth–early fifteenth centuries.
features.narration: East of Lake Chad, Kanem linked communities across the Sahara. Archaeologists now consider Tié a probable location of Njimi, its early Islamic capital.
features.architecture_gate: If depicting Tié at regional scale, use only a generic original fired-brick enclosure or building schematic. Its excavated elite building has plastered interior walls and a courtyard; a fully reconstructed palace skyline would exceed the checked evidence.
excluded_claims: Kanem founded in one exact year
The early state and surviving brick enclosure began together

features.verified_route_description: From Guinea's highlands near Sierra Leone, the Niger runs northeast through Mali and its inland delta, bends southeast into Niger, follows the Niger–Benin border, and enters Nigeria. The Benue joins at Lokoja; the lower Niger then runs south into a branching delta on the Gulf of Guinea.
features.narration: The Niger begins in Guinea's highlands, arcs through the western Sahel, and turns toward the Atlantic. At Lokoja, the Benue joins its waters.
features.length_note: Editorial rounding: opened FAO page says about 4,100 km and ESA says 4,180 km. Avoid false exactness.
features.geometry_gate: These passages verify orientation and confluence, not an animation polyline, historical channel geometry, or exact confluence coordinates. A separate licensed geometry source remains necessary for drawing the route.

coordinate.meaning: Reference point of the Chadian Lake Chad Ramsar wetland, site1134; not the centre of the entire lake or a medieval shoreline
coordinate.uncertainty: Site-level reference at minute precision; no accuracy statement.

features.narration: Around Lake Chad, water and trade sustained societies across the central Sahel.
features.source_supported_geographic_claim: Lake Chad is shared by Chad, Niger, Nigeria and Cameroon. Its extent varies over time.
features.representation_gate: Use a locator label or qualified background water shape. The opened modern sources do not establish a thirteenth-century shoreline. The broad narration's trade clause comes from the Kanem sources, not Ramsar or NASA.
